rationale:
PINS the `imports` relationship type, which measured 0 edges on 400 production-path corpus files while `import_declaration` occurred 2,358 times across 429 of them (script/m14/tmp/scala-grammar-inventory.ts). Expectations are the Scala Language Spec ch.9 reading of each clause form, re-probed from the parse tree with script/m60/scala-imports-exports-oracle.ts and cross-checked against the same rules on 1,687 corpus keys, where the oracle and the analyzer agree 100%.

THE TARGET IS THE DEPENDENCY, NOT THE BOUND NAMES. `import a.b.{Set, Map => ImmutableMap}` depends on the package `a.b`; the names inside `{...}` are what the clause binds. The lane's `references` twin builds its target from `ImportInfo.module`, which appends the renamed selector and yields `a.b.ImmutableMap` — that edge is an AUDITED label and is deliberately left alone here, so this fixture pins only the new `imports` edges and says so in a forbid entry that the twin keeps its own spelling.

Also pinned: the wildcard clause's target is the package and never `.*`; an `as`-renamed clause keeps the ORIGINAL name (`import scala.concurrent.duration.FiniteDuration` shape); a `private object` and a nested `class Inner` are not part of the surface, so they carry no export edge.

CORRECTION recorded after the first run, because the fixture is worth more than the guess: `ImportInfo.module` for `import scala.collection.immutable.{Set, Map => ImmutableMap}` is `scala.collection.immutable.Map` (the RENAMED selector is appended by the legacy path) and for `import java.io.{File => JFile, FileInputStream => Stream}` it is `java.io.FileInputStream`. The first draft of this expectation guessed `.Set` and `java.io.File`, and the run said so. Those two rows are the twin's spelling and are pinned here deliberately, so a future change to the legacy path cannot pass silently — while the `imports` edges beside them carry the spec spelling (`scala.collection.immutable`, `java.io`), which is the whole point of the new type.

One more correction from the run, same reason: `import java.io.{File => JFile, FileInputStream => Stream}` gives the legacy `ImportInfo.module` the value `java.io.File.FileInputStream` — BOTH selector names appended to the path. The `imports` edge beside it is `java.io`, which is the dependency the Scala spec says the clause has. Pinning both is deliberate: the legacy path is an audited label, and a future correction to it has to move this row rather than slip past it.
